books.section: Unit 5: Toward the Civil War and Reconstruction (1844–1877)

primary_sources: Thomas Nast, “The Union as It Was — The Lost Cause, Worse than Slavery,” Harper’s Weekly, October 24, 1874

stimulus.text: Thomas Nast’s cartoon “The Union as It Was — The Lost Cause, Worse than Slavery,” Harper’s Weekly, October 24, 1874. A man marked “White League,” a rifle on his back, shakes hands with a hooded Klansman marked “K.K.” over a shield. Above them an eagle carries the words “The Union as It Was” and “This Is a White Man’s Government.” Inside the shield, a Black mother and father crouch over their baby in grief, while behind them a freedman hangs from a tree and a schoolhouse burns. A child’s primer lies dropped on the ground.
stimulus.source_note: Thomas Nast, “The Union as It Was — The Lost Cause, Worse than Slavery,” Harper’s Weekly, October 24, 1874, p. 878 (Library of Congress, LCCN2001696840). Public domain. Image viewed before writing; details described from the image itself.

source: original; stimulus as noted in stimulus.source_note
stem: The cartoon calls the scene “worse than slavery.” Which of the following best explains what Nast meant?

options.text: Slavery had given Black families more protection than freedom did.
options.misconception: Nast is not praising slavery; he is saying the terror after emancipation betrayed freedom’s promise.

options.text: The federal government had re-enslaved Black Southerners by law.
options.misconception: Background: no federal law re-enslaved anyone; the Fourteenth and Fifteenth Amendments still stood.

options.text: Freedom’s promise was being destroyed by murder and intimidation.
Black Southerners preferred slavery to the sharecropping system.
options.misconception: The cartoon shows a family in terror, not a family choosing slavery.

rationales.A: Nast is not praising slavery; he is saying the terror after emancipation betrayed freedom’s promise.
rationales.B: Background: no federal law re-enslaved anyone; the Fourteenth and Fifteenth Amendments still stood.
rationales.C: Under slavery, Black families suffered bondage; after emancipation, Nast shows them facing lynching, a burning school, and armed men who mean to rule by fear. The “worse” is that freedom itself was being murdered.
rationales.D: The cartoon shows a family in terror, not a family choosing slavery.
rationales.general:
1. The words “worse than slavery” sit over a skull, so Nast is measuring a new horror.
2. Under slavery the evil was bondage; here the evil is murder aimed at free people.
3. The lynching, the burning school, and the armed handshake all attack freedom itself.
4. Nast’s point is that a freedom no one will defend can be worse than the bondage it replaced.
Remember: a cartoon’s harshest phrase is usually aimed at the betrayal, not at the thing betrayed.
